687.title: The hungry ghosts
687.hook: in Chinese communities, the seventh month's offerings to hungry ghosts and lost souls
687.howItsDone: In Chinese communities during the seventh lunar month, families make offerings of food, incense and paper goods, temples hold rites to feed hungry ghosts, and some communities stage performances with front-row seats left empty for unseen guests.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Obon, welcome fires and the circle dance. Your line: they come home.

Singapore, the seventh month of the lunar calendar. On the sidewalks, small fires burn in metal bins, paper offerings curling into ash. Little piles of oranges, rice and incense sit along the curbs. In open-air tents, singers perform loud, cheerful shows, and the front row of seats is left empty. Those seats, people say, are for the guests you can't see. Yesterday, Moggallana's mother was one hungry ghost, and her son could help her. In Chinese communities, this whole month is for all the others: the ghosts nobody remembers.
screen: `THE SEVENTH LUNAR MONTH.` → `OFFERINGS ON THE CURB.` → `THE EMPTY FRONT ROW.`

segments.voice: In Buddhist teaching, hungry ghosts, peta in Pali, preta in Sanskrit, are one of the realms of rebirth: beings driven by craving so strong that nothing satisfies it. East Asian art pictures them with huge, empty bellies and throats as thin as a needle, always hungry, never able to swallow enough. Craving, made visible. The Pali canon already speaks of them. A short text, the discourse outside the walls, pictures dead relatives standing outside houses, at crossroads and by doorposts, returning to their old homes, waiting. When the living give food and drink and dedicate the merit to them, the ghosts rejoice. In China, these threads came together with older customs of honoring the dead. On the fifteenth night of the seventh month, Buddhist temples hold the Ullambana rites you heard about yesterday; Taoists keep the same night as the Zhongyuan festival. Often the two are woven together, and families may not draw a sharp line. In some temples, monks perform a ritual of feeding the hungry ghosts, scattering food and chanting so that it can reach beings who can't otherwise eat. Notice who the month is really for. Not only your own grandparents: the lost ones, who died far from home or with no one left to remember them. The festival is a public kindness toward strangers who can't say thank you.
screen: `PETA: ALWAYS HUNGRY.` · `HUGE BELLY, NEEDLE THROAT.` · `WAITING OUTSIDE THE WALLS.` · then, large: `FEED THE HUNGRY.`

segments.voice: First, notice hunger in yourself, any kind: for food, for attention, for something to be different, and see it without judging, like the ghost's thin throat. Then widen out to the hungry people near you: a shelter, a person on a corner, a neighbor stretched thin. Hold them a while, and wish them fed.

Your line: feed the hungry. Even the ones nobody remembers. That's six hundred eighty-seven days.

688.title: Pavarana
688.hook: at the rains' end monks invite each other to point out their faults
688.howItsDone: At the end of the rains retreat, Theravada monks gather and each in turn formally invites the community to point out his faults; lay communities in Thailand, Laos and Myanmar mark the same full moon with merit-making and festivals of light.

segments.voice: Yesterday: peta, the hungry ghosts, and the empty front row. Your line: feed the hungry.

Imagine your workplace holds a meeting at the end of the year. Everyone sits in a circle, and one by one, starting with the most senior, each says to the group: if you've seen me do anything wrong, or heard of it, or even suspected it, please tell me. Out of kindness, tell me. Most offices would rather do anything else. Buddhist monks have done exactly this at the end of every rains retreat for over two thousand years. It's called Pavarana, the invitation.
screen: `A CIRCLE AT YEAR'S END.` → `IF YOU SAW ANYTHING, TELL ME.` → `THE INVITATION.`

segments.voice: The Vinaya tells how it began. A group of monks spent a rains retreat together and, to avoid any quarrel, agreed not to speak to each other at all, all season. They got through it peacefully and went to tell the Buddha. He did not praise them. Living together like that, in silence to avoid friction, isn't living at ease, he said. Instead he set a practice. At the end of the rains, each monk invites the community to speak to him about anything seen, heard or suspected. Out of compassion, speak to me, the invitation goes, and if I see the fault, I will make amends. Each monk says it three times. Notice the three: seen, heard, suspected. Not just proven. You're inviting the uncomfortable thing someone wasn't sure enough to say. The Connected Sayings tell how the Buddha himself did it. At one Pavarana, sitting with five hundred monks, he invited them first: is there anything I have done, in body or in speech, that you would criticize? Sariputta answered for them: no, sir. The teacher went first. In Thailand, Laos and Myanmar, this full moon also brings festivals of light, candles, lanterns and boats of light on rivers, and in some places the story that the Buddha came down from heaven this very day, which comes in two days. But the core is a sentence: tell me my faults. It's a hard sentence, and a brave one, and it keeps a community honest.
screen: `SILENCE TO AVOID QUARRELS.` · `THE BUDDHA DIDN'T PRAISE IT.` · `SEEN, HEARD, SUSPECTED.` · then, large: `TELL ME MY FAULTS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who knows you well and wishes you well, and imagine asking them: is there anything I do that you think I should see? Notice what happens in the body, tightness or heat, and breathe with it. Then picture their answer arriving, and you taking it in calmly, with thanks.
Pavarana. The invitation at the end of the rains, when each monk asks the community to point out any fault seen, heard or suspected. Today's word.

689.title: Kathina, deeper
689.hook: cloth offered, a robe cut and sewn by the community within a day
689.howItsDone: In Theravada communities, lay people bring Kathina cloth and other gifts to a monastery in the month after the rains; the monks formally give the cloth to one of their number, and in Myanmar some temples hold overnight robe-weaving contests.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Pavarana, the invitation at the end of the rains. Your line: tell me my faults.

Late evening at a monastery in Myanmar. In a hall lit with bulbs, teams of young women sit at wooden looms, racing. They've been weaving since the night before. By dawn, the robes must be woven, finished and offered, and crowds come to cheer them on. It's a contest, and also something older: a gift that must be made in a single stretch of time. You met Kathina in your first year: the thirty monks in muddy robes at the end of the rains, and the Buddha's allowance of new cloth. Today, inside the ceremony itself.
screen: `LOOMS RACING THROUGH THE NIGHT.` → `DONE BY DAWN.` → `THE MUDDY ROBES, REMEMBERED.`

segments.voice: Kathina has a few rules that make it unlike any other gift. First, timing: it can be held only in the month after the rains retreat ends, and only at a monastery where monks have completed the retreat. Second, the cloth must be offered freely. Monks can't ask for it, hint at it, or arrange it. Lay people bring it, unasked, to the whole community, not to one monk. Third, the community decides. In a formal act, the monks agree together to give the cloth to one of their number, often someone whose robes are worn or who is respected for his conduct. The fourth rule is today's line: the robe must be made that very day. The old texts describe cloth washed, measured, cut, sewn, dyed and finished before dawn, with the whole community helping. In some places today the cloth arrives already made, and the community completes the formal act the same day. The Myanmar weaving contest, held on an autumn full moon, carries the old urgency in a new form. Why a single day? The texts don't explain. Some teachers point to what it does: it gathers everyone at once, lay and monastic, around one task no one person can do alone. The robe that comes out is ordinary cloth. What's special is the night everyone spent making it together.
screen: `ONLY AFTER THE RAINS.` · `CLOTH GIVEN UNASKED.` · `THE COMMUNITY CHOOSES ONE.` · then, large: `SEWN IN A DAY.`

segments.voice: Picture a piece of cloth in your hands with a loose button or a small tear, and the needle going in and out, slowly, each stitch a breath. Notice how mending asks for patience: you can't rush a stitch. If sewing isn't for you, picture one small thing in your home that needs repair, and fixing it carefully.
Kathina. The cloth offering after the rains: given unasked, given to one monk by the community's choice, and made into a robe in a single day. Today's word.
Your line: sewn in a day. Many hands, one night, one robe. Day six hundred eighty-nine, done.

690.title: Lhabab Duchen
690.hook: in Tibet, the day the Buddha descended after teaching his mother in heaven
690.howItsDone: On Lhabab Duchen, Tibetan Buddhists visit temples, make offerings, recite prayers and mantras, circle stupas and give generously; in Thailand the descent is remembered at the end of the rains with a large alms-giving ceremony.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Kathina, the looms racing through the night. Your line: sewn in a day.

The Buddha's mother, Maya, died seven days after he was born. He never knew her. The tradition tells a story about that loss. Many years later, after his awakening, the Buddha rose to a heaven where his mother had been reborn as a god, and spent a whole rains retreat there teaching her. Then he came back down. In Tibet, the day he came down is one of four great holy days of the year.
screen: `MAYA DIED SEVEN DAYS AFTER.` → `HE NEVER KNEW HER.` → `HE WENT UP TO TEACH HER.`

segments.voice: The story is told in the commentaries and later texts, with many variations. In the Theravada telling, the Buddha spent the rains in the Heaven of the Thirty-Three, where his mother, reborn among the gods, came to hear him, and he taught the higher teaching, the Abhidhamma. Each day, the story goes, he passed a summary to Sariputta on earth, which is one way the tradition explains how the Abhidhamma reached the world. When the rains ended, he descended at a place called Sankassa, on a staircase the gods made: by tradition a jeweled stair in the middle, with gold and silver stairs on either side, the gods Brahma and Sakka attending him. Crowds waited at the bottom. In Tibetan, Lhabab Duchen means 'the great occasion of the descent from the realm of the gods.' It falls on the twenty-second day of the ninth Tibetan month, usually in November. People visit temples, make offerings, recite, circle stupas and holy places, and give generously. In Thailand, the same descent is remembered at the end of the rains with a great alms round, where monks walk down a hill or steps, like the Buddha coming down to the waiting crowd. Notice the shape of the story. He went up to give his mother the best thing he had. Then he came back down, to the people waiting. He didn't stay in heaven.
screen: `A RAINS RETREAT IN HEAVEN.` · `TEACHING HIS MOTHER.` · `A STAIRCASE AT SANKASSA.` · then, large: `HE CAME DOWN.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind your mother, or whoever mothered you: a grandmother, an aunt, a foster parent, a teacher, a friend; if that relationship is painful or absent, choose someone else who cared for you, or simply wish well to all mothers. Picture giving them the best thing you have to give: time, a word of thanks, a kindness. Then picture coming back down to your ordinary day, carrying that warmth with you.
Lhabab Duchen. The Tibetan holy day of the Buddha's descent, after a rains retreat spent teaching his mother in heaven. Today's word.
Your line: he came down. Up for his mother, back down for everyone. Until tomorrow.

691.title: Bodhi Day
691.hook: December 8 in Japan: the awakening; Zen monasteries sit for a week
691.howItsDone: In Japanese Zen monasteries, Rohatsu sesshin is a week of intensive sitting in early December, often ending with an all-night sit; many Buddhist communities in the West mark Bodhi Day on December 8 with meditation and readings.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Lhabab Duchen, the stair at Sankassa. Your line: he came down.

Early December in a Zen monastery in Japan. It's cold. The meditation hall is often unheated. For the past week, the monks have been sitting from before dawn until late at night, with short breaks for meals, work and a little sleep. On the last night, in many monasteries, nobody lies down at all. They sit through until morning. Then, just before sunrise, someone looks up at the eastern sky, where one bright point is still shining.
screen: `DECEMBER IN A ZEN MONASTERY.` → `A WEEK OF SITTING.` → `THE LAST NIGHT, NO SLEEP.`

segments.voice: Rohatsu means 'the eighth day of the twelfth month.' In Japan, that's when the Buddha's awakening is remembered, and since Japan moved to the solar calendar, temples there keep it on December eighth. Other East Asian communities mark the eighth day of the twelfth lunar month, and in China it's a day for a sweet porridge, laba congee, recalling the milk-rice the Buddha was given before his awakening. Theravada lands keep the awakening with the birth and the passing, on Vesak. Different calendars, the same night under the tree. The Pali texts tell the night in three watches. In the first, the Buddha recalled his past lives. In the second, he saw how beings pass away and are reborn according to their deeds. In the last, he understood suffering, its cause, its end and the way, and his mind was freed. As the night ended, dawn came. Later tellings, especially in East Asia, add one detail that has become central in Zen: he looked up, saw the morning star, the planet Venus, low in the eastern sky, and awoke. Zen retells that moment again and again: a star he had seen many times, seen now completely. The Rohatsu retreat follows the same shape, a week building to a last night without sleep, ending at dawn. The monks aren't waiting for a star. They're practicing being awake when it rises.
screen: `THE EIGHTH DAY, TWELFTH MONTH.` · `THREE WATCHES OF THE NIGHT.` · `A STAR AT DAWN.` · then, large: `THE MORNING STAR.`

segments.voice: Picture the cold hall, the rows of cushions, the long last night, and feel the stillness of it. Then picture the sky just before dawn, dark blue, one bright point low in the east. Let your attention be as clear as that point.

692.title: Nirvana Day
692.hook: February 15 in East Asia: the Buddha's passing remembered
692.howItsDone: In Japan and many Mahayana communities, temples mark Nirvana Day (Nehan-e) around February 15 by hanging a painting of the Buddha's passing, chanting, and reading from the account of his last days; Theravada Buddhists remember the passing on Vesak.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Rohatsu, the night of awakening and the star at dawn. Your line: the morning star.

In a temple in Japan in mid-February, a huge painted scroll is unrolled and hung. In the middle, a man lies on his right side between trees, head resting on his hand. Around him, crowds are weeping: monks, kings, gods. And animals. An elephant on its back. A tiger. Birds, a snake, a crowd of creatures. It's called a nehan-zu, a picture of nirvana. And it isn't a picture of awakening. It's a picture of a death.
screen: `A SCROLL UNROLLED IN FEBRUARY.` → `THE ANIMALS WEEPING.` → `A PICTURE OF A DEATH.`

segments.voice: Buddhists use the word nirvana for two things. One is the awakening itself, the fire of craving going out, which yesterday remembered. The other is what happens when an awakened one dies: the final nirvana, parinirvana in Sanskrit, parinibbana in Pali. Nothing is left to be reborn. Nirvana Day remembers that second one. In Japan it's usually kept on February 15; other Mahayana communities keep it then too, or on February 8, or by the lunar calendar. In Theravada lands, the passing is kept on Vesak, with the birth and the awakening. Same event, different calendars. Now the story, from the Book of the Great Decease. The Buddha is eighty, and ill. He walks to Kusinara, a small town, and lies down between two sal trees. The text says the trees burst into flower out of season and dropped blossoms on him. His cousin Ananda goes off and weeps against a doorpost. The Buddha calls him back: hadn't he always taught that everything dear must change and part? Then he asks the monks three times if anyone has a last doubt. Nobody speaks. And then his last words, in Rhys Davids's translation: "Decay is inherent in all component things! Work out your salvation with diligence!" He doesn't hide his death. He uses it as the final lesson. On Nirvana Day, temples chant, read the story and sit; some make little dumplings or rice cakes. The point isn't grief. It's looking straight at an ending, with company.
screen: `TWO MEANINGS OF NIRVANA.` · `A PASSING ON TWO CALENDARS.` · `BETWEEN THE SAL TREES.` · `THE LAST WORDS AS A LESSON.` · then, large: `ALL THINGS END.`

segments.voice: Let one ending come to mind, not the hardest one you know: a school, a house, a friendship that drifted, a pet, a season of life. Look at it the way the scroll looks at the Buddha, plainly, with company around, and if grief comes, let it sit with you too; Ananda wept. At the end, come back to this breath, which is also ending, and the next one, which is beginning.
Nirvana Day. February 15 in East Asian Buddhism, remembering the Buddha's final passing, his parinirvana between the sal trees. Today's word.
Your line: all things end. Even a Buddha's life came to a close. See you tomorrow.

693.title: Losar
693.hook: the Tibetan new year: cleaning the house, new prayer flags, fresh starts
693.howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhist families prepare for Losar by cleaning their homes, then hang new prayer flags, visit monasteries and shrines, make offerings and visit relatives over the first days of the new year.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Nirvana Day, the passing between the sal trees. Your line: all things end.

In Tibetan homes, a few days before the new year, everybody grabs a broom. Corners get scrubbed. Old dust goes out the door. It closes a week of festivals: the hungry ghosts fed, monks inviting each other to name their faults, a robe sewn in a single day, the Buddha coming down from heaven, the morning star, the passing between the sal trees. Yesterday ended with an ending. So today the calendar turns over. Today is Losar.
screen: `EVERYBODY GRABS A BROOM.` → `A WEEK OF FESTIVALS.` → `AN ENDING, THEN A TURN.`

segments.voice: Losar is two Tibetan words: lo, year, and sar, new. It follows the Tibetan lunar calendar, so it moves, usually landing in February or early March. It's kept in Tibet and by Tibetans everywhere, and in Bhutan, Ladakh and the Himalayan communities of Nepal, sometimes on different dates. First comes the cleaning: in the last days of the old year, houses are cleaned top to bottom. On the twenty-ninth evening, many families eat a soup called guthuk, with dough balls hiding little objects inside. Find salt and you're said to be lazy; find chili and you're said to have a sharp tongue. Everyone laughs. Then leftover soup and a dough figure are carried out of the house, with the old year's troubles, and left at a crossroads. Next, the flags. Strings of prayer flags, blue, white, red, green and yellow, are printed with prayers and mantras, and over a year wind and sun fade them to rags. At Losar many families take down the old ones and hang new ones on rooftops and passes. In Tibetan custom, the wind carries the blessings printed on them out to every being it touches. Then the visits. Monasteries hold special rituals and masked dances. Families visit shrines, make offerings, and greet each other with tashi delek, good fortune. Many historians think parts of Losar are older than Buddhism in Tibet, and that Buddhist practice and those older customs grew up together. Losar takes yesterday's line seriously, and then picks up a broom. The old year is really over, so you clear it out, and begin.
screen: `LO, YEAR. SAR, NEW.` · `CLEANING OUT THE OLD YEAR.` · `NEW FLAGS FOR THE WIND.` · `VISITS AND TASHI DELEK.` · then, large: `A FRESH YEAR.`

segments.voice: Picture one corner of your home, one drawer or one shelf, and what's piled there from a year that's already gone. In your mind, lift each thing, wipe the dust, keep what's useful and let go of what isn't. Notice the feeling of space when it's done.
